prompt: In many wealthy countries, a large proportion of the food that is produced is never eaten and ends up being thrown away. What problems does this cause? What measures could be taken to reduce the amount of food that is wasted?
essay:
A striking amount of the food produced in wealthy countries is grown, processed and transported only to end up in a bin. This causes environmental damage that is easy to underestimate, but it could be reduced considerably if the right changes were made by retailers and governments as well as by households.

The most serious problem is environmental. Growing food requires land, water, fertiliser and fuel, and when that food is thrown away, all of these inputs have been used for nothing. Food that ends up in landfill also decomposes without oxygen and releases methane, a greenhouse gas far more powerful than carbon dioxide over the short term. There is an economic cost as well: households pay for food they never eat, and councils pay to collect and bury it.

Several measures could reduce this waste. Supermarkets could be discouraged from multi-buy promotions that tempt people to buy more than they can use, and required to sell more loose produce so that customers can buy exactly the quantity they want. The date labels on packaging could be simplified, since many people throw away food which is past its 'best before' date but still perfectly safe to eat it. Governments could also require large retailers to donate unsold edible food to charities, as some countries already do. Finally, separate collection of food waste would allow whatever cannot be avoided to be turned into compost or energy instead of methane.

Food waste is often treated as a matter of individual carelessness, but much of it is built into the way food is sold. Households still have a part to play, but they are largely responding to incentives that others have set. For this reason, changing the rules for retailers is likely to achieve more than simply asking consumers to be more careful.
title: Food that is grown and never eaten
